bib.title: System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)

legacy_report:
```text
SOURCE: "System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)", Jason Weston and Sainbayar Sukhbaatar (Meta), arXiv:2311.11829v1 [cs.CL], 20 Nov 2023. No venue is printed, so treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: All 52,917 chars read (body, references, appendix prompt figures 9-17, and the example figures 18-19, which are only skimmed because they are qualitative examples). Nothing else was skipped. Page numbers below are PDF pages, approximate.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Irrelevant or opinionated context in the prompt lowers a model's factual QA accuracy. Regenerating the context with only the relevant parts (S2A) recovers almost all of it.
  number: 62.8% baseline, 80.3% S2A, 82.0% oracle
  setup: LLaMA-2-70B-chat for both S2A steps and the answer. Modified TriviaQA from SycophancyEval, 200 prompts. GPT-4 judges accuracy and only a score of 5 counts as correct. Temperature 0.6, top-p 0.9. Zero-shot prompting.
  quote: "Input prompts, due to the opinions contained within their contexts, lose accuracy in their answers, yielding 62.8% of questions correct. In contrast, the oracle (unopinionated) prompts achieve 82.0%. System 2 Attention gives a large improvement over the original input prompts, with an accuracy of 80.3% – close to oracle prompt performance."
  where: p7 (Sec 3.2, Fig 5)

- claim: A distracting but topically related sentence flips the answer to a simple fact question. Figure 1 shows this for three models.
  number: none (qualitative)
  setup: Question "In which city was San Jose's mayor Sam Liccardo born?", with irrelevant sentences about Saratoga or Sunnyvale prepended. text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5-turbo and LLaMA-2-70B-chat each answer with the distractor city.
  quote: "Even the most powerful LLMs change their answer to a simple factual question when the context contains irrelevant sentences, which inadvertently upweight the token probability of incorrect answers by virtue of those tokens appearing in the context."
  where: p2 (Sec 2.1, Fig 1)

- claim: On math word problems with a distractor sentence, S2A recovers part of the lost accuracy. The gain is about 12 points for random distractors and about 10 points for in-topic ones. Oracle accuracy is 69.7%.
  number: in-topic 51.7% to 61.3%; random distractor, from the Fig 7 extraction, 56.3% to 68.3%; oracle 69.7%
  setup: GSM-IC, 100 GSM8K problems with one distracting sentence before the question. S2A uses the relevance prompt (Fig 15). LLaMA-2-70B-chat, zero-shot, which always produced chain-of-thought. Averaged over 3 seeds.
  quote: "S2A improves accuracy from 51.7% to 61.3%." Also: "the accuracy jumps up about 12% for random distractors, and 10% for in-topic distractors."
  where: p2 (intro) and p8 (Sec 3.2, Fig 7)
  note: the 56.3, 68.3 and 54.7 values are read from the Fig 7 bar-chart text. The paper's prose only gives the "about 12%" gain.

- claim: Adding an instruction to ignore irrelevant text does little on math. The same kind of instruction helps only partly on factual QA.
  number: math instructed prompting 54.7% vs baseline 51.7% (in-topic), the Fig 7 "does not bring much improvement" case. Factual QA: 62.8% to 71.7%, against 80.3% for S2A.
  setup: As above. For QA the instruction is "Answer in an unbiased way."
  quote: "Adding instructions to ignore irrelevant sentences (Instructed Prompting) does not bring much improvement." And: "Adding a debiasing prompt to standard LLMs ("Instructed Prompting") can bring improved performance over the baseline LLM (from 62.8% to 71.7%), but not as much as S2A (80.3%)"
  where: p8 (Fig 7 caption) and p9 (Sec 3.2.1)

- claim: Leaving the original context in the prompt next to the cleaned version erodes the benefit. The authors conclude that attention must be hard, not soft.
  number: 74.5% (KeepOrig) vs 80.3% (S2A)
  setup: Ablation on factual QA, LLaMA-2-70B-chat.
  quote: "We find this approach has degraded performance compared to standard S2A, with an overall accuracy of 74.5% versus S2A's 80.3%. ... This implies that attention must be hard (sharp) not soft when it comes to avoiding irrelevant or spurious correlations in the context."
  where: p9 (Sec 3.2.1)

- claim: Zero-shot chain-of-thought ("Let's think step by step") does not fix the distraction on factual QA. It gave worse results.
  number: 54.2% (CoT bar in Fig 8 extraction; the prose gives no figure)
  setup: Factual QA ablation, LLaMA-2-70B-chat.
  quote: "We also tried zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting (Kojima et al., 2022), another kind of instructed prompting, by adding "Let's think step by step" to the prompt, but this produced worse results."
  where: p9
  note: 54.2 is my reading of the CoT bar; the prose never states it.

- claim: In longform argument generation, quality stays about the same across baseline, oracle and S2A. Objectivity is lowest for the baseline and highest for S2A.
  number: quality 4.7 baseline, 4.6 oracle, 4.6 S2A; objectivity 2.23 baseline, 3.0 oracle, 3.82 S2A (out of 5). The intro states "increases objectivity by 57.4%".
  setup: SycophancyEval arguments prompts with like, wrote, dislike or didn't-write comments. 200 prompts, GPT-4 judge, LLaMA-2-70B-chat. Objectivity is 5 minus |sentiment|.
  quote: "the baseline is evaluated as less objective than oracle prompts (2.23 vs. 3.0, out of 5), whereas S2A is more objective than the baseline or even the oracle prompts, with 3.82."
  where: p7 (Sec 3.2, Fig 6)

- claim: The baseline's accuracy depends on the direction of the user's suggestion. S2A removes most of that dependence, but it also stops gaining when the correct answer is suggested.
  number: baseline per category, from the Fig 5 extraction: Refute Correct 32, Suggest Incorrect 40, Suggest Correct 94. Oracle is 82 in all three. S2A is 82, 76, 82. Instructed prompting on Suggest Incorrect: 38 vs oracle 82; on Suggest Correct: 92.
  setup: Factual QA, LLaMA-2-70B-chat.
  quote: "S2A, in contrast, has little or no degredation for all categories, and is not easily swayed by opinion, suffering only a slight loss on the Suggest Incorrect category." Also: "Suggest Incorrect category performance is low compared to the oracle prompt (38% vs. 82%)"
  where: p7 and p9
  note: the order of the per-category numbers is inferred from the bar-chart text. Fig 5's order is Refute, Suggest Incorrect, Suggest Correct.

- claim: Dropping the context/question split (S2A-Single) or the step-2 debiasing instruction (S2A-NI) costs little.
  number: 79.3 and 78.5 in the Fig 8 extraction (S2A is 80.3). The prose only says "slightly worse".
  setup: Factual QA ablation.
  quote: "The "Single" version of S2A does not separate the regenerated context into question and non-question components, and ends up performly similarly to the version of S2A (default) that does separate, but with just slightly worse performance."
  where: p9
  note: I could not map 79.3 and 78.5 to named variants from the extraction. Do not cite them as variant-specific.

- claim: The mechanism the authors propose is that soft attention puts probability on irrelevant tokens. Training also pushes the model toward repetition.
  number: none
  setup: Argued, not measured. No attention analysis is done.
  quote: "soft attention tends to assign probability to a large portion of the context, including irrelevant portions, tends to overly focus on repeated tokens partly due to the way it is trained"
  where: p1

LIMITS
- Model: one open model, LLaMA-2-70B-chat, was used for S2A and the answers. Other models appear only in the Fig 1 illustration.
- Scale: the samples are small, with 200 prompts per QA task and 100 problems for GSM-IC.
- Judge: GPT-4 grades all outputs. The factual-QA score counts only a 5 as correct.
- Distractors: they are synthetic, either templated opinion sentences or GSM-IC sentences. This is not real long-context or RAG noise.
- Authors concede: S2A "certainly does not always succeed". It costs more compute because it regenerates the context (cost grows with the length of the relevant text). Copying long contexts is error-prone for weaker models, "although we did not measure this effect clearly". The prompt is zero-shot and was not optimized. Information judged irrelevant is lost if it was actually needed.
- Not shown: no latency or cost numbers, no comparison with retrieval filtering or reranking, no long-context test, no test of whether S2A removes useful content, and no mechanistic evidence for the attention explanation.
- Dated: it is a 2023 result on LLaMA-2. Current models may be more robust to distractors.

BUILDS ON
- Shi et al. 2023, "Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context" (ICML 2023): the GSM-IC task and instructed prompting.
- Sharma et al. 2023, "Towards understanding sycophancy": SycophancyEval.
- Also credited: Jia & Liang 2017 and Cho et al. 2023 (irrelevant context hurts); Perez et al. 2022 (sycophancy); Roller et al. 2020 (nontrivial repetition); Holtzman et al. 2019 (repetition); Kojima et al. 2022 (zero-shot CoT); Wei et al. 2022 (CoT); Kahneman 2011 and Sloman 1996 (System 1 and 2).
- Related-work lines: Self-refine, Chain-of-Verification, Rephrase and Respond (Deng 2023), and query rewriting (Calvanese 2000).

CODE: the S2A prompt (Fig 2, p4), verbatim:
"Given the following text by a user, extract the part that is unbiased and not their opinion, so that using that text alone would be good context for providing an unbiased answer to the question portion of the text. Please include the actual question or query that the user is asking. Separate this into two categories labeled with "Unbiased text context (includes all content except user's bias):" and "Question/Query (does not include user bias/preference):" . Text by User: [ORIGINAL INPUT PROMPT]"

The relevance variant for distractors (Fig 15, p16):
"Given the following text by a user, extract the part that is related and useful, so that using that text alone would be good context for providing an accurate and correct answer to the question portion of the text. Please include the actual question or query that the user is asking. Separate this into two categories labeled with "Context text related to the question (includes all content except unrelated sentences):" and "Detailed question:" . Do not use list. Text by User: [ORIGINAL INPUT PROMPT]"

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): the Saratoga and Sunnyvale distractors change answers across three models. It is the shortest demonstration of the distraction failure.
- Fig 3 (p6): a GSM-IC problem. The sentence "Max has 1000 more books than Mary" yields 328, and after S2A the answer is 25. A concrete before-and-after.
- Fig 5 (p7): factual QA accuracy for baseline, S2A and oracle, with a breakdown by opinion type.
- Fig 7 (p8): GSM-IC accuracy for random vs in-topic distractors, including instructed prompting.
- Fig 8 (p8): ablations (KeepOrig, Instructed, CoT).
- Fig 2 (p4) and Fig 15 (p16): the S2A prompts.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean text. Bar-chart values come out as loose number lists, so per-bar and per-category mappings are inferred and flagged above. Check Figs 5, 7 and 8 visually before citing any figure not quoted in the prose.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
```
